extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent practitioners (attorneys/agents), and applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on identifying statutory and nonstatutory (obviousness-type) double patenting, when the doctrine applies, and how to address obviousness-type rejections (primarily via terminal disclaimer) including strategic and procedural considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory ("Same Invention") Double Patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the same invention is claimed in two patents/applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory double patenting cannot be overcome by a terminal disclaimer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonstatutory ("Obviousness-Type") Double Patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Where claims are not patentably distinct from claims in another commonly owned patent/application (a judicial doctrine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This type of double patenting can be obviated by filing a terminal disclaimer that meets regulatory requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for When Double Patenting Applies (common ownership/entity factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness-type double patenting occurs when applications have: the same inventive entity; at least one common inventor; a common applicant; a common owner/assignee; or are owned by parties to a joint research agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of these common-ownership or common-entity relationships is an element in analyzing obviousness-type double patenting rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness-Type Test: Lack of Patentable Distinctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Double patenting (obviousness-type) is present when claims in the later application are not patentably distinct from claims in an earlier commonly owned patent/application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims for patentable distinctness (i.e., whether one claim would have been obvious over the other). If not distinct, an obviousness-type double patenting rejection is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Policy Rationale for Nonstatutory Double Patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: The nonstatutory-type rejection is grounded in public policy and primarily intended to prevent prolongation of the patent term by prohibiting claims in a second patent not patentably distinct from claims in a first patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also intended to prevent harassment by multiple assignees of patents covering essentially the same invention; these policy goals inform application of the doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal Disclaimer as a Remedy for Obviousness-Type Rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent applicant or patent owner may obviate nonstatutory double patenting by filing a terminal disclaimer meeting the requirements of 37 CFR 1.321(c) or (d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing a proper terminal disclaimer is the primary procedural mechanism to overcome obviousness-type double patenting rejections; ensure compliance with the cited CFR provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal/Regulatory Requirements for Terminal Disclaimers (37 CFR 1.321(c)/(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Terminal disclaimer must meet the statutory/regulatory requirements set forth in 37 CFR 1.321(c) or (d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page references these specific CFR provisions as the controlling requirements—practitioners should consult the text of 37 CFR 1.321(c)/(d) for exact formalities and content required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of Filing a Terminal Disclaimer
rubrics_metrics.description: By filing a terminal disclaimer, the patent applicant agrees that the later-filed patent (if granted) expires when the first patent does and that the patent will only be enforceable while both patents are commonly owned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These limiting concessions are material to enforcement and licensing strategies; applicants should weigh the loss of term and ownership constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-Way Test for Double Patenting (limited circumstances)
rubrics_metrics.description: In limited circumstances (where applicant could not have filed both inventions in the same application due to actions of the PTO), a 'two-way' obviousness test applies — both patents must be obvious in light of each other for double patenting to apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the two-way test only when PTO actions prevented concurrent claiming; both directions of obviousness must be established to sustain the double patenting rejection under this test.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO Rulemaking and Policy Developments (2024 proposals)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO proposed rules requiring an agreement that the patent with the terminal disclaimer will be enforced only under certain conditions, but this proposal generated significant pushback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of recent and proposed changes to terminal disclaimer practice and enforcement terms; monitor rulemaking and stakeholder responses that may affect how disclaimers are implemented or interpreted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic Consequences: Loss of Patent Term
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing a terminal disclaimer can lose patent term (later patent expires earlier).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should consider the commercial impact of a shortened term before filing a terminal disclaimer; terminal disclaimers trade enforceability for co-terminosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic Consequences: Common Ownership and Licensing/Assignment Impact
rubrics_metrics.description: The common ownership requirement can affect licensing/assignment because the disclaimer ties enforceability to common ownership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must consider how licensing or assignment transactions will affect enforceability when a terminal disclaimer is in place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Restriction Requirements and 35 U.S.C. 121 Safe Harbor
rubrics_metrics.description: Restriction requirements protect against double patenting in continuations/divisionals (35 USC 121 safe harbor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When restriction requirements apply, 35 U.S.C. 121 may provide a safe harbor from double patenting—consider restriction practice and divisional/continuation strategy to mitigate double patenting risks.
